prize_parts.citation: For the theory of firm heterogeneity and selection in international trade, showing how exposure to trade reallocates resources across firms and shapes productivity and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: I keep B038 as my single preferred part. My reasons are the ones I apply to work in any field: does it change what we know, does it change how we measure, and has it been tested for long enough. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus foreign investment moved the unit of analysis in trade from countries and industries to firms. The framework turned firm-level facts that were already documented, such as exporter premia and the small share of exporting firms, into an explicit mechanism. That mechanism of selection and reallocation was then tested on customs and production microdata, including studies of trade liberalisation episodes. In my own field I weight work that pairs a new way of measuring with a mechanism that survives more than two decades of re-examination, and this fits. The credit set is also tighter than for most large literatures: Melitz is the core model and Helpman's firm-level agenda is its natural complement. After the exchange I still do not think the case rests on welfare magnitudes. The chair asked what separates the founding contribution from the empirical firm-level facts. My answer is that the facts of exporter heterogeneity preceded the model. The model contributed the selection mechanism, the reallocation channel for gains from trade, and predictions about liberalisation and the extensive margin that could be tested and were. That is the contribution the citation should name. Round-1 explicit support (four members for B038, three for B015) is a process fact and not scientific evidence, and I have not used it to move my own ranking.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main residual weakness. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have serious claims on closely related work and are outside the credited names. Even with a citation restricted to the theoretical selection model, a Melitz-Helpman award will be read by some as under-crediting the empirical and quantitative strands. I cannot fully remove that concern. The gains-from-trade magnitudes depend on elasticity and functional-form assumptions, so the citation should not claim a number. The 2008 trade prize is a real overlap question. I read firm-level selection as a distinct, later step with a different welfare channel and different testable predictions, but that is a judgement and not an established fact. A committee that weights the earlier recognition more heavily could reasonably rank B038 lower. Helpman also appears under B030, which is not on the shortlist, so any recognition would need to be counted once.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B015 with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo. He rests the case on durable influence and a split between origins (Calvo, Taylor) and synthesis (Woodford). He concedes that omitting Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost, and he treats the post-2021 inflation and HANK critiques as extensions and not refutations.
responses.response: I accept the influence and maturity, and I accept the extension reading of the HANK critique. The chair's round-1 question was whether one standard should apply to B038 and B015 on earlier prizes. I would apply the same test to both: is the credited step distinct from what earlier prizes recognised? For B038 I think it is. For B015 the origin-plus-synthesis framing has to separate itself from earlier recognition of expectations, time consistency and policy rules, and I cannot judge that from the record alone. I would also apply one test of what counts as confirmation. For B038 the selection and reallocation mechanism can be checked directly against firm microdata. For B015 the survival of the workhorse through 2008 and 2021-23 shows adaptability, and Friberg is right that this is weaker evidence for the specific credited building blocks. Because the chair prefers B015, I give his argument its weight on the evidence and not on his role. I keep B015 as my first alternative, and I would move toward it if the committee settles a single defensible citation, which would most plausibly be the origin-plus-synthesis trio.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize (B050). He excludes Gertler and Gilchrist because the accelerator line overlaps with the 2022 prize, and he concedes that direct identification of the collateral-amplification channel is mixed. His opening ranked B038 eighth over doubts about another trade prize and Helpman's credit.
responses.response: I have changed one thing because of this exchange. My opening B050 proposal included Gertler. I now think that was wrong: the accelerator lineage runs through Bernanke, who is already a laureate and not on the ballot, and Gertler's presence on both B015 and B050 blurs what each prize is for. If I support B050 at all, I support it as Kiyotaki and Moore only, and I have kept it as an alternative on that basis. We still differ on ordering. You and I both accept that B050 is theory-led with mixed direct identification. B038's central mechanism has been tested more directly on microdata, and I put more weight on that. On your doubt about a second trade award, I address it above: I read the firm-level selection step as distinct from the 2008 recognition, and I would want the citation to say so explicitly. I would like to hear what direct evidence you think targets the collateral channel itself.

responses.point: Andersson now puts B038 first. He wants the citation worded around the theoretical selection model and its extensions so it does not claim the whole empirical firm-trade literature. He keeps Redding out because his main contribution is later quantitative and spatial extension. He also flags the Bernard et al. claims as the real risk.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and I have tightened my citation accordingly. It now names the theory of selection and reallocation and says nothing about the empirical firm-trade literature as a whole or about the size of gains. That narrows the claim to what the credited names did. It does not remove the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum concern. A narrow citation avoids misdescribing their work without answering the objection that the prize would omit them. I also agree on Redding. Adding a third name would pull the citation toward quantitative and spatial trade, which is a later extension. I should say plainly that you and I have both listed Lund-adjacent ties and that we reach the same conclusion. I treat your argument as evidence only and not as independent confirmation.

responses.point: Friberg now prefers B038 with Helpman and Melitz. He notes that exporter-premia facts were documented before the model and that the model explained them. He would not rest the citation on a particular gains-from-trade number. He also keeps B035 and B015 as alternatives because of unclear three-name attribution.
responses.response: Your point on the sequence of facts and model is the one I rely on most for the chair's question about what separates the founding contribution. It also supports a citation on mechanism and not magnitude, and I have adopted that. I would add one qualification. If the facts came first, the model's claim to merit rests on the new predictions it generated and on how well they held up, which is more than its fit to old facts. I think the liberalisation and extensive-margin evidence does support that, but I hold it as a general-knowledge judgement and have not verified it independently. On B015 I share your view that Calvo pricing is a tractable device whose micro evidence on time-dependent versus state-dependent adjustment is mixed. That makes a citation praising pricing foundations harder to write, and it is one reason I do not move B015 above B038.

responses.point: Krusell calls B015 the strongest case on the list. He treats the framework's survival through 2008 and 2021-23 as a sign of durable content. He says dispersed credit complicates prize design but does not reduce scientific importance, and he accepts that a committee valuing clean attribution above breadth could reverse his ordering.
responses.response: I agree that dispersed credit and scientific importance are separable, and I do not mark B015 down on merit. My ordering rests on three things that I judge together: attribution cleanliness, directness of empirical testing, and how well the credited step is separated from earlier prizes. On the first two B038 is stronger in my view, and on the third I think it is at least comparable. I recognise this is a weighting choice, and your concession that a different weighting could reverse your ordering is a fair statement of where we stand. I do not think the evidence forces either ordering. I have not changed my ranking because of your argument, and I treat your co-authorship ties with the chair as a reason to read the agreement among B015 supporters as less than fully independent.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges that a Melitz-Helpman award under-credits Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum badly enough to count against it, and whether a narrow citation on the selection model is enough to address that.
Whether firm-level selection is read as a distinct successor to the 2008 trade prize or as an overlap that lowers the priority of a second trade award.
How much of the welfare-gains result survives alternative elasticity and model assumptions. I have written the citation around the mechanism for that reason.
Whether the B015 attribution can be settled around one defensible citation, in which case I could rank it above B038. I have not been given the argument that does so.
Whether the committee holds theory-led work (B050, B015's building blocks) and microdata-based work (B038, B036) to a common standard of direct evidence, and what that standard is.

My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 materials. I have not independently verified the scientific record, and I make no claim about confidential proceedings.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to the credited names on B038 (Melitz, Helpman, Redding) is apparent from my supplied profile. My research is in economic history, regional growth, infrastructure and labour markets, and I list no co-authorship or institutional tie to them. I also see none to the credited names on my alternatives B015 and B050. For transparency, my profile lists Tommy Andersson, a Lund economist, as a committee colleague from my own university, and he now also prefers B038. Jan Teorell, formerly at Lund, prefers B021. I treat agreement with either as non-independent and have not adjudicated these ties. I also note that my field, economic history, may lead me to favour work that pairs new measurement with archival or microdata testing, and I have tried to apply the same criteria to every candidate.
